transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Yeah, hi. I guess the main thing is… I keep running into this wall with work that takes real sitting-down brain effort. Like monthly reports, or planning a multi-site health event — stuff I know is important, and I’m not careless about it, I mean I work in health services so details matter — but I just keep putting it off.

And it’s weird because I can be busy all day, answering people, handling little issues, you know, someone needs something fixed right now and I’m on it. But when it’s the bigger planning or paperwork where I have to sit and think through it, I sort of… avoid it. Then suddenly I’m reorganizing emails or checking on some other thing that probably could’ve waited. That’s really why I’m here.
Have you had this same kind of trouble focusing on effortful tasks since childhood?

Yeah, I mean… I think so. My mom used to tell this story from elementary school where the teachers would say I was bright, like I understood things, but I was always sort of staring out the window or off in my own world.

And I’d lose worksheets constantly. Homework too — not always doing it, but sometimes doing it and then not turning it in, which sounds ridiculous. My mother ended up checking my backpack every night because otherwise something would just sit in there crumpled up. She had this whole routine by the front door, actually, with folders and—yeah, sorry. But yes, it was there when I was a kid too.
Do you have the same kind of trouble getting started on effortful tasks at home?

Yeah, I mean… at home it’s kind of the same pattern, though the work examples are the ones that made me finally come in. Anything that needs me to sit down and really think through it, like reports or planning something with a lot of moving parts, I just hit this wall.

I’ll know it matters, and I’m not trying to blow it off, but I keep putting it off and then somehow I’m doing something else that feels useful but isn’t the thing. It’s frustrating because I can be busy, but not actually doing the hard mental task I needed to start.
Do you often lose or misplace everyday things like keys, your phone, or paperwork?

I’m not totally sure. I mean, everybody loses keys sometimes, right? I don’t know if mine is more than normal. I do have moments where I’m looking around for something and then I realize I set it down somewhere odd, but I haven’t really kept track of it.

Paperwork is… maybe a little different, but I don’t know if that counts as losing it or just not having a great system. At work there are so many folders and emails and printed forms, and then someone interrupts you and—sorry, I’m wandering. I guess my honest answer is I haven’t really noticed losing everyday things as a major issue.
Do you spend a lot of time worrying about many different things, even when there isn’t an immediate problem to solve?

I’m not sure I’d say a lot of time, no. I mean, I worry about things when there’s actually something going on — work stuff, family stuff, bills, whatever — but I don’t think I’m sitting around worrying about everything all the time.

Sometimes I can get stuck thinking about something, but… I don’t know, that feels more like I’m trying to remember what I was supposed to do next, not exactly worrying. Sorry, that may not be what you meant. So I guess my answer is: I haven’t really noticed constant worry like that.
When you put off a task, is it often because you feel it needs to be done exactly right before you can start?

Not really because it has to be perfect, no. I mean, I do want things done correctly, especially in healthcare admin where there are a lot of details and people depending on the plan, but that’s not the main thing.

It’s more like… if it’s something that takes real sit-down brain work, I just hit a wall. Monthly reports are a big one, or planning a multi-site health event where there are a bunch of moving parts. I’ll know it matters, I’ll even have the files open sometimes, and then I somehow end up doing smaller things around it instead. Like I’m busy, but not actually starting the thing that needs the most thinking.
Have these problems with starting and finishing effortful tasks caused trouble at work?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, I’m still functioning, I still go to work and people generally see me as reliable enough, but there have been times where something I was supposed to move forward just kind of sat there too long.

And then—sorry, this is probably more detail than you need—but in healthcare admin there’s always another email or a meeting or someone needing a quick answer, and I’ll do those things, but the bigger task doesn’t get finished. Then a coworker has to step in or remind me, or the deadline slips and I’m sending those embarrassing last-minute apologies like, “Sorry, I’m getting this to you now.”

It’s happened outside work too, with friends, where I’m late finishing something I said I’d help with. So yes, I’m getting by, but it has caused some trouble.
Outside of work, do you have the same trouble starting tasks that take a lot of mental effort?

Yeah, outside of work too. It’s the same kind of thing where if something needs me to sit down and really think through steps, I sort of… stall out.

Like, at work it’s monthly reports or planning a big multi-site event, but at home it can be anything that feels like it needs that same brain effort. I’ll know it matters, and I’ll tell myself, “Okay, just start,” and then somehow I’m doing some smaller easier thing instead.

It’s not that I don’t care about it. It feels more like I hit this wall before I even get going.
In social situations, do you often find your mind drifting and miss parts of what people are saying to you?

Yeah, that happens. In social situations, and honestly in meetings too, I’ll be trying to listen and then something small pulls me off.

Like if someone’s giving a budget update, I’m looking at them and trying to follow, but then a phone vibrates, or people are talking out in the hall, or I suddenly remember something I forgot to do for the league—sorry, I coach with this local thing, so that pops into my head—and then I realize I missed the next few minutes of what was being said.

It’s embarrassing because I’m physically there, nodding along, but then I have to piece together what I missed.
Did these concentration and procrastination problems get noticeably worse after a specific stressful event at work or in your personal life?

Yeah… I think there was a shift. It’s been about, I guess, almost two years now—like a year and eleven months—since my friend died.

After that I ended up taking on more with the league and some outreach stuff, because he had been involved in a lot of that, and I don’t know… it just all kind of expanded. I remember thinking I could keep all the plates spinning, and for a while I was just saying yes to things because it felt like the right thing to do.

So I don’t know if it was one clean moment where everything got worse, but since then, that’s when I really started noticing the concentration and procrastination being more of a problem.
Have these focus and procrastination problems caused trouble in managing everyday responsibilities outside work, like bills, appointments, or household tasks?

Yeah, it has. Not always huge things, but enough that it causes problems.

Like with the league and community stuff, I’ll forget to return calls from volunteers, and then by the time I remember it’s awkward because they were waiting on me for something. Or I’ll be on my way to do one errand for an event and somehow miss the smaller thing I was supposed to pick up too.

And once or twice, which I felt really bad about, a community meeting just completely slipped my mind until somebody texted me like, “Are you coming?” I mean, I try to keep track of things, but if it’s not right in front of me, it can just kind of disappear.
Do thoughts about your friend’s death keep pulling your attention away from what you’re trying to do?

Not exactly thoughts about him, no—not usually in that direct way. It’s more like I’ll be trying to pay attention, like in a meeting when someone’s going over a budget update, and then something small pulls me off.

A phone vibrates, or people are talking out in the hallway, or I suddenly think, “Oh, I forgot to handle that thing for the league,” and then I’m gone for a few minutes mentally. By the time I snap back, I’ve missed part of what was said.

So it can be league-related, and all of that connects back in some way, I guess, but it’s not always like I’m sitting there thinking about his death. It’s more my attention just gets yanked away.
As a child, did adults often say you didn’t seem to listen when spoken to directly?

Yeah, I think so. I mean, the way my mom tells it, even back in elementary school the teachers would say I was bright, but I was always kind of… off somewhere else. Daydreaming, I guess.

And there was this whole routine with my backpack—my mother had to check it every night because I’d lose worksheets or just forget to turn in homework. I’d have it done sometimes, but it would still be sitting crumpled in a folder or at the bottom of my bag. So yeah, adults definitely noticed something like that when I was a kid.
As a child, were you often fidgety or unable to stay seated when you were expected to?

I’m not really sure on that one. I don’t remember being the kid who was constantly getting out of his seat or running around the room or anything like that.

My mom told more stories about me zoning out than bouncing off the walls. I mean, I probably squirmed like any kid, especially if class was boring, but I don’t know that adults saw me as fidgety in that way. I’d have to ask her, honestly.
Do these attention problems also affect you in settings other than work, like at home or in community activities?

Yeah, it does. I mean, I’m still functioning, I guess — I’m not falling apart or anything — but it shows up outside work too.

Like with the league stuff, or even just with friends, I’ll miss something I was supposed to follow up on, and then I’m sending some embarrassed text at the last minute like, “Sorry, I totally dropped this.” And at work it’s similar — people have had to cover little gaps for me, or remind me about things, and some deadlines have slipped.

It’s frustrating because from the outside it probably looks like I don’t care, but I do. I’m just kind of always trying to catch up after my attention goes somewhere else.
Do you often have trouble organizing tasks and activities?

Yeah, organizing is a big one for me. Like, when I’m juggling work projects and then the memorial committee stuff and outreach events, I’ll have notes in three different places — my phone, a notebook, some random email I sent myself — and then I can’t figure out what actually needs to happen first.

And then somehow everything feels equally urgent, so I kind of spin around with it until suddenly it’s the end and I’m rushing to pull it together. Which, I mean, I usually do get something done, but it’s stressful and messier than it should be.
As a child, did you often avoid or put off schoolwork because it felt like it took too much mental effort?

Yeah… I think so, though I remember it more as this feeling of just hitting a wall when something needed real sitting-down brain work.

Like schoolwork, especially if it was a long assignment or something where I had to read and then write something thoughtful, I’d put it off and put it off. It’s kind of the same thing now with monthly reports or planning one of those bigger multi-site health events — I know it matters, I know I need to do it, but my brain just sort of refuses to start.

And then I’ll do other “useful” things instead, like cleaning up emails or organizing papers, which makes me feel like I’m being productive, but really I’m avoiding the thing that takes the heavier mental effort.

Not exactly thoughts about him, no—not usually in that direct way. It’s more like I’ll be trying to pay attention, like in a meeting when someone’s going over a budget update, and then something small pulls me off.

A phone vibrates, or people are talking out in the hallway, or I suddenly think, “Oh, I forgot to handle that thing for the league,” and then I’m gone for a few minutes mentally. By the time I snap back, I’ve missed part of what was said.

So it can be league-related, and all of that connects back in some way, I guess, but it’s not always like I’m sitting there thinking about his death. It’s more my attention just gets yanked away.

doctor.intent: Differentiate ADHD from an adjustment-related concentration problem by testing for another core childhood inattentive symptom beyond procrastination.
doctor.question: As a child, did adults often say you didn’t seem to listen when spoken to directly?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Even in elementary school, my teachers told my parents I was bright but always daydreaming, losing worksheets, and forgetting to turn in homework unless my mother checked my backpack every night.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about whether similar attention-related problems were present in childhood, which matches the onset-before-age-12 profile.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I think so. I mean, the way my mom tells it, even back in elementary school the teachers would say I was bright, but I was always kind of… off somewhere else. Daydreaming, I guess.

And there was this whole routine with my backpack—my mother had to check it every night because I’d lose worksheets or just forget to turn in homework. I’d have it done sometimes, but it would still be sitting crumpled in a folder or at the bottom of my bag. So yeah, adults definitely noticed something like that when I was a kid.

doctor.intent: Differentiate lifelong ADHD from a stress-related adjustment problem by checking for another core childhood ADHD symptom beyond inattention.
doctor.question: As a child, were you often fidgety or unable to stay seated when you were expected to?

target_item.reason: The question asks about childhood hyperactivity/restlessness, specifically fidgeting or being unable to stay seated, but the provided symptom profile does not include that symptom.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure on that one. I don’t remember being the kid who was constantly getting out of his seat or running around the room or anything like that.

My mom told more stories about me zoning out than bouncing off the walls. I mean, I probably squirmed like any kid, especially if class was boring, but I don’t know that adults saw me as fidgety in that way. I’d have to ask her, honestly.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the symptoms are occurring across multiple settings, which helps distinguish longstanding ADHD from problems limited to work stress or adjustment issues.
doctor.question: Do these attention problems also affect you in settings other than work, like at home or in community activities?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m still getting by at work and in the community, but people have had to cover gaps for me, deadlines have slipped, and I’ve embarrassed myself with last-minute apologies to coworkers and friends.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the attention problems cause impairment across multiple settings, including home and community activities, not just work.

patient.answer:
Yeah, it does. I mean, I’m still functioning, I guess — I’m not falling apart or anything — but it shows up outside work too.

Like with the league stuff, or even just with friends, I’ll miss something I was supposed to follow up on, and then I’m sending some embarrassed text at the last minute like, “Sorry, I totally dropped this.” And at work it’s similar — people have had to cover little gaps for me, or remind me about things, and some deadlines have slipped.

It’s frustrating because from the outside it probably looks like I don’t care, but I do. I’m just kind of always trying to catch up after my attention goes somewhere else.

doctor.intent: Differentiate chronic ADHD from a stress-related adjustment problem by testing for another core inattentive symptom independent of procrastination.
doctor.question: Do you often have trouble organizing tasks and activities?

target_item.name: Organization_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: When I’m juggling work projects, memorial committee stuff, and outreach events, I have notes in three different places and I can’t seem to figure out what needs to happen first, so I end up rushing at the end.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about trouble organizing tasks and activities, which matches this symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Yeah, organizing is a big one for me. Like, when I’m juggling work projects and then the memorial committee stuff and outreach events, I’ll have notes in three different places — my phone, a notebook, some random email I sent myself — and then I can’t figure out what actually needs to happen first.

And then somehow everything feels equally urgent, so I kind of spin around with it until suddenly it’s the end and I’m rushing to pull it together. Which, I mean, I usually do get something done, but it’s stressful and messier than it should be.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there are enough childhood inattentive symptoms to support ADHD rather than adjustment-related or work-related problems.
doctor.question: As a child, did you often avoid or put off schoolwork because it felt like it took too much mental effort?

target_item.name: Sustained_Mental_Effort_Avoidance
target_item.manifestation: The main reason I’m here is that anything that takes real sitting-down brain work, like monthly reports or planning a multi-site health event, feels like I hit a wall and I keep putting it off even when I know it matters.
target_item.reason: The question is directly asking about avoiding or putting off schoolwork because it required too much mental effort, which matches sustained mental effort avoidance.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think so, though I remember it more as this feeling of just hitting a wall when something needed real sitting-down brain work.

Like schoolwork, especially if it was a long assignment or something where I had to read and then write something thoughtful, I’d put it off and put it off. It’s kind of the same thing now with monthly reports or planning one of those bigger multi-site health events — I know it matters, I know I need to do it, but my brain just sort of refuses to start.

And then I’ll do other “useful” things instead, like cleaning up emails or organizing papers, which makes me feel like I’m being productive, but really I’m avoiding the thing that takes the heavier mental effort.

inference.note: Childhood onset and cross-situational inattentive symptoms are now well established, including poor listening/daydreaming, losing or not turning in schoolwork, avoidance of sustained mental effort, organizational problems, distractibility, and current impairment across work, home, and community settings. Generalized worry and perfectionism are not supported, and the bereavement-related worsening appears to be an exacerbating stressor rather than the primary disorder. Z56.9 is not a diagnosis explaining the syndrome.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's chief concern in their own words to guide the diagnostic interview.
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The interview supports ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation: longstanding inattention and executive dysfunction beginning in childhood, present across multiple settings, and causing functional impairment. Confirmed symptoms include difficulty sustaining attention, seeming not to listen/daydreaming, disorganization, avoidance of sustained mental effort, forgetfulness, and childhood academic/task follow-through problems. Hyperactivity symptoms were not endorsed, making inattentive type most consistent. Anxiety, perfectionism, and grief-related attentional problems were considered less likely because the patient denied pervasive worry, denied perfectionistic avoidance as the main cause, and stated attention is not primarily pulled away by intrusive thoughts about the friend's death.
